claim: Twenty-nine adults participated in the experiment, recruited from the UCL Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience subject pool.
source: Twenty-nine adults participated in the experiment, recruited from the UCL Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience subject pool.
evidence: Direct statement in the Materials and methods section describing participant recruitment.

claim: Three participants were excluded before the start of analysis for large movement or myographic artifacts.
source: Three were excluded before the start of analysis for large movement or myographic artifacts.
evidence: Direct statement in the Materials and methods section describing exclusion criteria.

claim: Of the 26 remaining participants, age quartiles were 18.7, 19.5, 21.3, 26.7, 41.4 years.
source: Of the 26 remaining, age quartiles were 18.7, 19.5, 21.3, 26.7, 41.4 years
evidence: Direct statement providing demographic data of the final participant sample.

claim: 14 of the 26 participants were female.
source: 14 were female
evidence: Direct statement providing demographic data of the final participant sample.

claim: 1 of the 26 participants was left-handed.
source: 1 was left-handed
evidence: Direct statement providing demographic data of the final participant sample.

claim: Subjects were not aware of the Si–Sd pairings in the Association phase.
source: As in Wimmer and Shohamy (2012), debriefing revealed that subjects were not aware of the Si–Sd pairings.
evidence: Direct statement based on debriefing data, with citation to similar finding in prior work.

claim: Subjects exhibited a strong preference for Sd+ over Sd− (p = 6.9 × 10−4).
source: Subjects exhibited a strong preference for Sd+ over Sd− (p = 6.9 × 10−4)
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test result, supported by Figure 1B showing behavioral data.

claim: As a group, subjects showed no evidence of preferring Si+ over Si− (p = 0.9).
source: as a group showed no evidence of preferring Si+ over Si− (p = 0.9)
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test result, supported by Figure 1B showing behavioral data.

claim: The change in relative liking from before to after the experiment was more positive for Sd+ than Sd− (p = 0.04).
source: The change in relative liking from before to after the experiment was more positive for Sd+ than Sd− (p = 0.04, one-sample t-test)
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test result, supported by Figure 1B showing liking rating changes.

claim: There was no significant difference between the changes in liking for Si+ and Si−.
source: but there was no significant difference between the changes for Si+ and Si−
evidence: Direct statement about statistical comparison, supported by Figure 1B showing liking rating changes.

claim: Many occipital and temporal sensors first became predictive of Si category between 90 and 230 ms post stimulus onset.
source: Many occipital and temporal sensors first became predictive of Si category between 90 and 230 ms post stimulus onset
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 2A showing sensor-level timing of category discrimination.

claim: Some parietal and frontal sensors became predictive of Si category ranging from 330–550 ms post stimulus onset.
source: followed by some parietal and frontal sensors ranging from 330–550 ms post stimulus onset
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 2A showing sensor-level timing of category discrimination.

claim: At 200 ms post-stimulus, the 95th percentile of the null distribution was 35.0% accuracy.
source: At 200 ms post-stimulus, the 95th percentile of the null distribution was 35.0% accuracy
evidence: Direct statement providing statistical threshold from permutation testing.

claim: At 200 ms post-stimulus, the median of the null distribution was 33.7% accuracy.
source: the median was 33.7%
evidence: Direct statement providing statistical threshold from permutation testing.

claim: Two distinct peaks in multivariate classification performance were observed, one centered approximately around 200 ms and the other around 400 ms post-stimulus onset.
source: We observed two distinct peaks in multivariate classification performance, one centered approximately around 200 ms and the other around 400 ms post-stimulus onset.
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3A showing classification accuracy over time.

claim: At the group level, the quadratic term in the regression of classification accuracy against time was significantly different from zero (p = 0.02).
source: At the group level, the quadratic term was significantly different from zero (p = 0.02).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test result testing for concavity in classification accuracy.

claim: No individual subject reached Bonferroni-corrected significant betas on the quadratic term of the regression.
source: many subjects trended toward a positive quadratic term, but none reached significance at a Bonferroni-corrected threshold
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing individual subject regression results.

claim: At 200 ms after Si onset, there was no difference in representational similarity between same-category and different-category Si objects (p = 0.2).
source: At 200 ms, the activity patterns evoked by stimuli within a category were no more similar than those evoked by stimuli in different categories (Figure 3B, left panel; p = 0.2, paired t-test between subjects)
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test result, supported by Figure 3B left panel showing representational similarity matrix.

claim: At 400 ms after Si onset, representational similarity was higher for same-category than different-category objects (p = 5 × 10−7).
source: whereas at 400 ms, patterns within a category were substantially more similar than between categories (Figure 3B, right panel; p = 5 × 10−7)
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test result, supported by Figure 3B right panel showing representational similarity matrix.

claim: Cross-validated performance of a linear SVM in 6-way discrimination of fractal identity was sharply peaked at 160 ms post-stimulus onset.
source: we found that the cross-validated performance of a linear SVM in a 6-way discrimination of fractal identity was sharply peaked at 160 ms post-stimulus onset
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3C showing classification accuracy for fractal identity over time.

claim: Fractal identity discrimination lacked a substantial second peak.
source: and lacked a substantial second peak
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3C showing classification accuracy for fractal identity over time.

claim: Classifiers trained around 200 ms post-Si presentation achieved above-chance accuracy in predicting which Si category had previously been associated with the presented Sd from 270–530 ms following presentation of Sd.
source: We observed that the classifiers trained around 200 ms post-Si presentation achieved above-chance accuracy in predicting which Si category had previously been associated with the presented Sd (the 95th percentile of the peak-level achieved in 200 random shuffle tests is shown as a solid black line in each panel). This effect was above chance from 270–530 ms following presentation of Sd.
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4A showing cross-classification results.

claim: The spatial pattern of brain activity present 200 ms after presentation of Si in the Association phase was partially reinstantiated 270–530 ms after presentation of Sd in the Reward phase.
source: In other words, the spatial pattern of brain activity present 200 ms after presentation of Si in the Association phase was partially reinstantiated 270–530 ms after presentation of Sd in the Reward phase.
evidence: Direct interpretation of cross-classification results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Classifiers trained around 400 ms after Si achieved above-chance accuracy in predicting the Si category previously associated with the Sd presented on trials at 70 ms following presentation of the outcome.
source: The classifiers trained around 400 ms after Si achieved above-chance accuracy in predicting the Si category previously associated with the Sd presented on this trial (Figure 4B). This effect was strongest at 70 ms following presentation of the outcome
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4B showing cross-classification results.

claim: The spatial pattern of activity present 400 ms after presentation of Si in the Association phase was at least partially reinstantiated 70 ms after presentation of the outcome in the Reward phase.
source: meaning that the spatial pattern of activity present 400 ms after presentation of Si in the Association phase was at least partially reinstantiated 70 ms after presentation of the outcome in the Reward phase
evidence: Direct interpretation of cross-classification results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Two-way ANOVA revealed no significant main effects of 200 ms vs 400 ms or Sd vs outcome but a significant interaction (p = 0.04).
source: Two-way ANOVA revealed no significant main effects of 200 ms vs 400 ms or Sd vs outcome but a significant interaction (p = 0.04; Figure 4C).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test result, supported by Figure 4C showing peak classification accuracies.

claim: The peak accuracy following Sd was higher for the 200 ms than the 400 ms classifier.
source: That is, the peak accuracy following Sd was higher for the 200 ms than the 400 ms classifier
evidence: Direct statement interpreting the interaction effect, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: The peak accuracy following outcome was higher for the 400 ms than the 200 ms classifier.
source: while the peak accuracy following outcome was higher for the 400 ms than the 200 ms classifier
evidence: Direct statement interpreting the interaction effect, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: There is a double dissociation in the component that was more strongly retrieved at Sd vs outcome.
source: implying a double dissociation in the component that was more strongly retrieved at Sd vs outcome
evidence: Direct interpretation of the interaction effect shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A linear SVM was reliably able to classify whether a spatial pattern of sensor contributions belonged to Sd or outcome (71.2% accuracy, p = 0.002 by one-sided binomial test).
source: Prediction accuracy reached 71.2%, which was greater than chance by one-tailed binomial test (p = 0.002).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test result, supported by Figure 5 showing spatial patterns of sensor contributions.

claim: The information about the category of Si retrieved at the time Sd was presented emerged primarily from occipital sensors.
source: Intriguingly, the information about the category of Si retrieved at the time Sd was presented emerged primarily from occipital sensors (A)
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5A showing sensor contribution patterns.

claim: The information about the category of Si retrieved at the time the outcome was shown appeared more strongly in parietal and temporal sensors.
source: while the information about the category of Si retrieved at the time the outcome was shown appeared more strongly in parietal and temporal sensors (B)
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5B showing sensor contribution patterns.

claim: In the difference between Sd and outcome sensor patterns, no individual sensor survived correction for multiple comparisons.
source: In the difference between the two conditions, no individual sensor survived correction for multiple comparisons.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical testing of spatial patterns.

claim: In subjects preferring Si+ over Si−, reinstatement of the 200 ms component of Si was strongly correlated with behavioral preference.
source: Remarkably, in subjects preferring Si+ over Si−, reinstatement of the 200 ms component of Si was strongly correlated with behavioral preference.
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 6B,D,F showing correlation analysis.

claim: The 200 ms classifier showed a corrected-significant peak in correlation strength ∼400 ms after the onset of the outcome.
source: while the 200 ms classifier showed a corrected-significant peak in correlation strength ∼400 ms after the onset of the outcome (Figure 6D)
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 6D showing correlation time course.

claim: The 400 ms classifier showed no substantial positive correlation with behavioral preference.
source: The 400 ms classifier showed no substantial positive correlation with behavioral preference (Figure 6C)
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 6C showing correlation time course.

claim: Retrieval of representations through associative links induces reinstantiation of at least some aspects of the pattern of neural activity evoked by the original presentation.
source: Retrieval is classically linked to reinstantiation of a particular distributed spatial pattern of neural activity mirroring that evoked by the original experience of the object or context being retrieved (Tulving and Thomson, 1973; Nyberg et al., 2000; Hoffman and McNaughton, 2002; Polyn et al., 2005; Johnson and Rugg, 2007; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2008; Danker and Anderson, 2010; Rissman and Wagner, 2012; Miller et al., 2013; Kuhl and Chun, 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior literature establishing this principle.

claim: When an object is directly experienced, the evoked pattern of neural activity evolves rapidly over tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
source: However, electrophysiology experiments robustly demonstrate that when an object is directly experienced, the evoked pattern of neural activity evolves rapidly over tens to hundreds of milliseconds (Makeig et al., 1997; Schmolesky et al., 1998, 1998; Näätänen and Winkler, 1999; VanRullen and Thorpe, 2001; Rossion and Jacques, 2008; Schneider et al., 2008; Cichy et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior electrophysiology literature.

claim: Direct experience of an object evokes multiple distinct spatial patterns of neural activity in sequence.
source: This implies that direct experience of an object evokes multiple distinct spatial patterns of neural activity in sequence.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation that neural activity evolves rapidly over time.

claim: These distinct spatial patterns have never been identified independently at retrieval.
source: However, these distinct spatial patterns have never been identified independently at retrieval.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the current work relative to prior literature.

claim: EEG studies provide evidence that some information is retrieved as early as 300 ms following a cue.
source: EEG studies provide evidence that some information is retrieved as early as 300 ms following a cue (e.g., Johnson et al., 2008; Yick and Wilding, 2008; Wimber et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior EEG literature.

claim: Manning et al. (2011), (2012), using electrocorticography, and Jafarpour et al. (2014), using MEG, showed that oscillatory patterns are also reinstated during retrieval.
source: Manning et al. (2011), (2012), using electrocorticography, and Jafarpour et al. (2014), using MEG, showed that oscillatory patterns are also reinstated during retrieval
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior electrocorticography and MEG literature.

claim: In two studies, the predominance of low oscillatory frequencies in reinstatement suggests a potential spectral signature.
source: in two of these studies the predominance of low oscillatory frequencies in reinstatement suggests a potential spectral signature
evidence: Statement about findings from cited studies, with inference about spectral signature.

claim: The dynamics of representation during direct experience of an object have never been tied to the dynamics of retrieval.
source: However, the dynamics of representation during direct experience of an object have never been tied to the dynamics of retrieval.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the current work relative to prior literature.

claim: It is not known which of the patterns evoked in sequence by direct experience are reinstantiated during retrieval.
source: It is not known which of the patterns evoked in sequence by direct experience are reinstantiated during retrieval
evidence: Statement about gaps in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: It is not known what the temporal relationship is in retrieval of patterns evoked by direct experience.
source: what the temporal relationship is in their retrieval
evidence: Statement about gaps in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: It is not known what functional significance the temporal structure of retrieval has.
source: or what functional significance this has
evidence: Statement about gaps in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Recent advances in multivariate methods for MEG have greatly improved our ability to discern fast-changing distributed representations in humans.
source: Recent advances in multivariate methods for MEG have greatly improved our ability to discern fast-changing distributed representations in humans (Carlson et al., 2013; Cichy et al., 2014; Jafarpour et al., 2013, 2014; van de Nieuwenhuijzen et al., 2013; Sandberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to recent methodological literature.

claim: Sensory preconditioning is a well-established paradigm in which subjects first form an association between two stimuli and then form an association between the direct stimulus and a reward.
source: Sensory preconditioning is a well-established paradigm in which subjects first form an association between two stimuli ('direct' or Sd and 'indirect' or Si) and then form an association between the direct stimulus and a reward (Brogden, 1939).
evidence: Statement defining the paradigm with citation to foundational work.

claim: Generalization of value to the indirect stimulus is evidence of retrieving the learned association.
source: Generalization of value to the indirect stimulus is evidence of retrieving the learned association (Gewirtz and Davis, 2000).
evidence: Statement about interpretation of behavioral results with citation to prior work.

claim: Using fMRI, Wimmer and Shohamy (2012) showed that neural representations of the associated indirect stimulus are reinstated when direct stimuli are presented during the Reward-learning phase.
source: Using fMRI, Wimmer and Shohamy (2012) showed that neural representations of the associated indirect stimulus are reinstated when direct stimuli are presented during the Reward-learning phase
evidence: Statement about findings from cited fMRI study.

claim: Retrieval of the indirect stimulus through the learned associative link is linked to the generalization of value from direct to indirect stimuli.
source: and this retrieval is linked to the generalization of value from direct to indirect stimuli
evidence: Statement about findings from Wimmer and Shohamy (2012) study.

claim: Reinstatement through the learned associative link may be part of the mechanism for value updating.
source: This suggests that reinstatement through the learned associative link may be part of the mechanism for value updating.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings from Wimmer and Shohamy (2012).

claim: The neural representation of the indirect stimulus can be decomposed into at least two temporal components with distinct properties.
source: We show that the neural representation of the indirect stimulus can be decomposed into at least two temporal components with distinct properties
evidence: Summary statement of main finding from the current study.

claim: The two temporal components of the indirect stimulus representation are retrieved at different times during the Reward-learning phase.
source: and these are retrieved at different times during the Reward-learning phase
evidence: Summary statement of main finding from the current study.

claim: The retrieval of only one of the temporal components is correlated with a behavioral measure of the generalization of value across the learned associations.
source: The retrieval of only one of these components is correlated with a behavioral measure of the generalization of value across the learned associations.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding from the current study.

claim: The temporal structure within retrieved neural representations may be key to their function.
source: We suggest the temporal structure within retrieved neural representations may be key to their function.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: MEG was recorded continuously at 600 samples/second using a whole-head 275-channel axial gradiometer system.
source: MEG was recorded continuously at 600 samples/second using a whole-head 275-channel axial gradiometer system (CTF Omega, VSM MedTech, Canada)
evidence: Direct statement about MEG acquisition parameters.

claim: The 600 samples in each epoch were reduced to 50 time bins by averaging together each consecutive 12 samples.
source: The 600 samples in each epoch were then reduced to 50 time bins by averaging together each consecutive 12 samples.
evidence: Direct statement about data preprocessing.

claim: The time bins were spaced every 20 ms and represented the average raw signal of the 12 samples within that 20 ms.
source: Thus, the time bins were spaced every 20 ms and represented the average raw signal of the 12 samples within that 20 ms.
evidence: Direct statement about data preprocessing.

claim: The regularization parameter C was tuned to optimize cross-validation performance in cross-validation of Association-phase data (C = 105).
source: The regularization parameter C was tuned to optimize cross-validation performance in cross-validation of Association-phase data (C = 105)
evidence: Direct statement about SVM parameter selection.

claim: All (Association) time*(Reward) time maps of classification performance were smoothed by a 2-D Gaussian kernel (σ = 30 ms).
source: All (Association) time*(Reward) time maps of classification performance were smoothed by a 2-D Gaussian kernel (σ = 30 ms) for display and for calculating peak-level shuffling statistics.
evidence: Direct statement about data analysis procedures.

claim: The randomization of Si–Sd pairings across subjects makes exceedingly unlikely the possibility that some visual features of Si happen to be shared with the associated Sd.
source: Note that the randomization of Si–Sd pairings across subjects makes exceedingly unlikely the possibility that some visual features of Si happen to be shared with the associated Sd and might therefore carry a shared neural signature.
evidence: Statement about experimental design controlling for confounds.

claim: The outcome always appeared 3500 ms after Sd in each trial.
source: Since the outcome always appeared 3500 ms after Sd in each trial
evidence: Direct statement about task timing.

claim: 70 ms after presentation of outcome was equivalently 3570 ms after presentation of Sd.
source: 70 ms after presentation of outcome was equivalently 3570 ms after presentation of Sd
evidence: Calculation based on task timing.

claim: All the information necessary to retrieve Si was carried by Sd.
source: Since all the information necessary to retrieve Si was carried by Sd
evidence: Statement about task structure and information content.

claim: Some of the retrieval process might occur before onset of the outcome.
source: some of the retrieval process might occur before onset of the outcome
evidence: Speculative statement about timing of retrieval processes.

claim: Both forms of cross-classification were very much less accurate than classification of the identity of the Sd or outcome from the activity directly evoked by these stimuli.
source: Both forms of cross-classification were very much less accurate than (linear) classification of the identity of the Sd (fractals) or outcome (coin/blue square) from the activity directly evoked by these stimuli (cf. Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Comparative statement about classification accuracies across different analyses.

claim: The relatively precise epoch of retrieval of Si following the presentation of the outcome may reflect the point of strongest overlap between a variety of timings in individual subjects.
source: The relatively precise epoch of retrieval of Si following the presentation of the outcome may reflect the point of strongest overlap between a variety of timings in individual subjects.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of timing results.

claim: A representation that is latent may have become detectable as soon as more power arose in the visual-evoked ERF due to onset of the outcome.
source: Alternatively, it may be that a representation that is latent became detectable as soon as more power arose in the visual-evoked ERF due to onset of the outcome.
evidence: Speculative alternative interpretation of timing results.

claim: Expectations of the next stimulus may partly drive representations in the first 10s of milliseconds after a visual onset, before the present stimulus is processed.
source: Yet another possibility is expectations of the next stimulus partly drive representations in the first 10 s of milliseconds after a visual onset, before the present stimulus is processed.
evidence: Speculative alternative interpretation of timing results.

claim: Retrieved representations (perhaps especially those that subjects are not consciously aware of) may be weak compared to evoked representations.
source: The low accuracy in classifying retrieved representations (∼35%) compared to evoked responses (∼60%) might imply that retrieved representations (perhaps especially those that subjects are not consciously aware of) were weak compared to evoked representations.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of classification accuracy differences.

claim: Si representations may have been only retrieved on a subset of trials, weakening the average signal.
source: It is also possible that Si representations were only retrieved on a subset of trials, weakening the average signal.
evidence: Speculative alternative interpretation of classification accuracy.

claim: Retrieved representations may have had a distributed spatial pattern that was only partly overlapping with the evoked representation, making it more difficult to detect with pattern classifiers trained on evoked activity.
source: Finally, it is possible that retrieved representations had a distributed spatial pattern that was only partly overlapping with the evoked representation, making it more difficult to detect with pattern classifiers trained on evoked activity.
evidence: Speculative alternative interpretation of classification accuracy.

claim: If the 400 ms component of Si representation preferentially encodes information about category rather than specific stimuli, retrieval of solely this component at outcome time might cause value learning to be assigned to categories rather than individual stimuli.
source: If the 400 ms component of Si representation preferentially encodes information about category rather than specific stimuli, as suggested by our representational similarity analysis, retrieval of solely this component at outcome time might cause value learning to be assigned to categories rather than individual stimuli.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about mechanism of value learning based on representational structure.

claim: This hypothesis would explain the finding that subjects who retrieve the 200 ms component at outcome show behavioral evidence of sensory preconditioning.
source: This hypothesis would explain our finding that the subjects who retrieve the 200 ms component at outcome show behavioral evidence of sensory preconditioning.
evidence: Speculative explanation connecting hypothesis to behavioral results.

claim: The correlation that Wimmer and Shohamy found in BOLD between retrieved stimulus representations and behavior between subjects may have been driven by the 200 ms component of the stimulus representation.
source: Under this interpretation, the correlation that Wimmer and Shohamy found in BOLD between retrieved stimulus representations and behavior between subjects may also have been driven by the 200 ms component of the stimulus representation
evidence: Speculative reinterpretation of prior fMRI findings in light of current results.

claim: Temporally precise signals could not be distinguished using fMRI.
source: these temporally precise signals could not be distinguished using fMRI
evidence: Statement about methodological limitations of fMRI relative to MEG.

claim: The finding that exact timing of reward relative to fast-evolving neural representational structures is crucial to value updating and credit assignment is of general importance.
source: the finding is of general importance because it suggests that the exact timing of reward relative to fast-evolving neural representational structures is crucial to value updating and credit assignment
evidence: Statement about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: Training a classifier to distinguish between individual exemplars of an Si category did not reach a sufficiently high level of performance.
source: Although it is in principle possible to train a classifier to distinguish between individual exemplars of an Si category, this did not reach a sufficiently high level of performance in our hands
evidence: Statement about attempted but unsuccessful analysis.

claim: The inability to classify individual exemplars may be limited by the relatively small number of training samples per unique stimulus.
source: perhaps limited by the relatively small number of training samples per unique stimulus
evidence: Speculative explanation for unsuccessful analysis.

claim: Offline and online processes may share similar mechanisms.
source: Offline and online processes may share similar mechanisms (Doll et al., 2014)
evidence: Statement with citation to prior work on offline/online processing.

claim: In some cases the division between offline and online mechanisms is blurred.
source: and in some cases the division between offline and online mechanisms is blurred
evidence: Statement about conceptual issues in distinguishing processing types.

claim: Retrieving elements of past experiences may serve as part of the process of planning in advance for the next time related situations are encountered.
source: For example, retrieving elements of past experiences may serve as part of the process of planning in advance for the next time related situations are encountered (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011, 2013), similar to the psychological notion of implementation intentions (Gollwitzer, 1999).
evidence: Statement with citations to prior work on planning and implementation intentions.

claim: In sensory preconditioning, it is an open question whether generalized values are updated offline, retrieved through associative links at the time of decision, or a mix of both.
source: In sensory preconditioning, it is an open question whether generalized values are updated offline (either during the Reward phase or in between the Reward and Decision phases), retrieved through associative links at the time of decision, or a mix of both.
evidence: Statement about unresolved questions in the field.

claim: In animals the vulnerability of sensory preconditioning to extinction hints at an online mechanism.
source: In animals the vulnerability of sensory preconditioning to extinction (Gewirtz and Davis, 2000) hints at an online mechanism
evidence: Statement with citation to animal literature, making inference about mechanism.

claim: It is equally possible that extinction drives offline value updates through the same generalization mechanism as acquisition.
source: but it is equally possible that extinction drives offline value updates through the same generalization mechanism as acquisition
evidence: Speculative alternative interpretation of extinction effects.

claim: The representation of Sd may have changed through the associative learning so that it more closely resembles that of Si.
source: Indeed, although our description of the reinstatement of Si suggests that it arises through a distinct process of retrieval, we cannot distinguish this from the subtly different possibility hinted by these ideas that the representation of Sd changed through the associative learning so that it more closely resembles that of Si.
evidence: Speculative alternative interpretation of the cross-classification results.

claim: In animals, the temporal structure of retrieval appears to subserve complex memory, learning and decision-making processes, especially in hippocampus and hippocampal–cortical interactions.
source: In animals, the temporal structure of retrieval appears to subserve complex memory (Sirota et al., 2003; Schwindel and McNaughton, 2011), learning and decision-making processes, especially in hippocampus and hippocampal–cortical interactions.
evidence: Statement with citations to animal literature on temporal structure of retrieval.

claim: Rodents retrieve representations of past and future locations, actions, and rewards.
source: Rodents retrieve representations of past and future locations, actions, and rewards (Johnson and Redish, 2007; van der Meer et al., 2010; Steiner and Redish, 2014)
evidence: Statement with citations to rodent literature on retrieval.

claim: The timing of retrieval in rodents is tightly structured and likely encodes critical information in the decision-making computation.
source: the timing of this retrieval is tightly structured and likely encodes critical information in the decision-making computation
evidence: Statement about rodent literature with inference about functional significance.

claim: In humans, frontal theta power is implicated in coding temporal order within sequences of stimuli.
source: In humans, frontal theta power (Hsieh et al., 2011) and patterns of activity in hippocampus (Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014; Hsieh et al., 2014) are implicated in coding temporal order within sequences of stimuli.
evidence: Statement with citations to human literature on temporal order coding.

claim: In humans, patterns of activity in hippocampus are implicated in coding temporal order within sequences of stimuli.
source: In humans, frontal theta power (Hsieh et al., 2011) and patterns of activity in hippocampus (Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014; Hsieh et al., 2014) are implicated in coding temporal order within sequences of stimuli.
evidence: Statement with citations to human literature on temporal order coding.

claim: Information in the visual system up to 200 ms post-stimulus may hew closely to the form of the stimulus that was presented.
source: Information in the visual system up to 200 ms post-stimulus may hew closely to the form of the stimulus that was presented (Tanaka and Curran, 2001; VanRullen and Thorpe, 2001; Liu et al., 2002; Schiff et al., 2006; Rossion and Jacques, 2008).
evidence: Statement with citations to visual neuroscience literature.

claim: Brain activity later than 200 ms post-stimulus is often found to include contextual and other sources of information.
source: Conversely, brain activity later than 200 ms post-stimulus is often found to include contextual and other sources of information (Kok, 2001; Tsivilis et al., 2001; Schiff et al., 2006; Garrido et al., 2007; Sanguinetti et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement with citations to literature on later visual processing.

claim: The N400 component of the ERP extends from roughly 250–500 ms post-stimulus and appears to be driven at least partly by the medial temporal lobe.
source: In particular, the N400 component of the event-related potential (ERP) in EEG extends from roughly 250–500 ms post-stimulus and appears to be driven at least partly by the medial temporal lobe, which is functionally coupled to sensory cortices (Bar, 2004).
evidence: Statement with citation about N400 component characteristics.

claim: The medial temporal lobe is functionally coupled to sensory cortices.
source: which is functionally coupled to sensory cortices (Bar, 2004)
evidence: Statement with citation about functional connectivity.

claim: The N2pc component of the ERP occurs from roughly 200–300 ms post-stimulus and has been tied to contextually-sensitive processing.
source: The N2pc component of the ERP, which occurs earlier from roughly 200–300 ms post-stimulus, has also been tied to contextually-sensitive processing (Conci et al., 2006; Schiff et al., 2006)
evidence: Statement with citations about N2pc component characteristics.

claim: The N2pc component originates from lateral temporal and parietal sources.
source: and originates from lateral temporal and parietal sources (Hopf et al., 2000; Oostenveld et al., 2001)
evidence: Statement with citations about N2pc source localization.

claim: The observation of more consistent category information at 400 ms may reflect contextually-sensitive processing based on lateral and top-down functional connections.
source: Although information about the category of our stimuli is directly available in their visual form, one interpretation of our observation of more consistent category information at 400 ms is that this reflects such contextually-sensitive processing happening based on lateral and top-down functional connections (MacKay and Bowman, 1969; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Ullman, 2000; Engel et al., 2001; Bledowski et al., 2006; Garrido et al., 2007; Friston and Kiebel, 2009; Kourtzi and Connor, 2011).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with extensive citations to literature on contextual processing.

claim: Timing of event-related signals depends strongly on stimulus properties.
source: Finally, we note that timing of event-related signals depends strongly on stimulus properties (e.g., Bobak et al., 1987).
evidence: Statement with citation about stimulus-dependence of timing.

claim: Multivariate classification yields different timings in the peaks of classification depending on the specific kinds of categories evaluated.
source: Multivariate classification also yields different timings in the peaks of classification depending on the specific kinds of categories evaluated (Cichy et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement with citation about category-dependence of classification timing.

claim: The particular temporal structure of evoked responses is most likely specific to the stimuli used.
source: Thus the particular temporal structure of evoked responses is most likely specific to the stimuli used.
evidence: Inference from cited literature about stimulus-specificity.

claim: Mapping the temporal structure of representations for a given task and stimuli can be leveraged to probe the dynamics of retrieval.
source: Mapping this structure for a given task and stimuli can be leveraged to probe the dynamics of retrieval.
evidence: Statement about methodological implications of the work.

claim: Neural retrieval of representations through associative links is central for memory and decision-making.
source: In summary, neural retrieval of representations through associative links is central for memory and decision-making.
